name: Sliggoo
smogon_description:
As far as special tanks go in NU, Sliggoo manages to hold its own thanks to a number of desirable traits, notably its unique mono-Dragon typing in conjunction with high special bulk, which enables it to check a myriad of threatening special attackers such as Magmortar, Rotom, and Life Orb Samurott. Sap Sipper furthers Sliggoo's walling capabilities, letting it serve as a hard counter to Lilligant without Hidden Power Ice, one of NU's most fearsome Pokemon, as well as granting it the ability to switch into Sleep Powder from the likes of Lilligant and Vivillon. Curse is another one of Sliggoo's main draws when compared to other special tanks in NU, as it is incredibly difficult to take down should it accumulate several boosts. Alternatively, Sliggoo can fulfill the role of an offensive tank thanks to a wide offensive movepool with a powerful STAB option in Draco Meteor and decent Special Attack to complement. However, Sliggoo relies on Eviolite in order to effectively switch into special attackers, making it vulnerable to the ever-present Knock Off and, to a lesser extent, Trick. Sliggoo also tends to take away offensive momentum from the team due to the nature of Rest + Sleep Talk. Lackluster Defense proves to be cumbersome as well, and somewhat difficult to manage in a metagame with influential physical attackers such as Kangaskhan, Tauros, and Rhydon.
Curse lets Sliggoo act as a bulky setup sweeper, making it increasingly difficult to break past with physical attacks. Outrage packs quite a punch after Sliggoo has gotten a couple Curse boosts under its belt. It also doesn't lock Sliggoo into the move if it's drawn by Sleep Talk. Rest lets Sliggoo stays healthy throughout the game and keeps it free of otherwise harmful status ailments such as poison and burn, while Sleep Talk ensures that Sliggoo is still functional during the turns when it's asleep.
The given HP and Special Defense EVs plus Eviolite grant Sliggoo enough special bulk to avoid the 3HKO from both Samurott's and Ludicolo's Ice Beam, as well as the 2HKO from Focus Sash Jynx's Ice Beam, while the rest goes into Defense to let it avoid the 3HKO from Tauros' Rock Climb after one Curse. Sap Sipper is chosen for the very useful immunity to Grass-type moves it provides, notably Sleep Powder, making Sliggoo a particularly good switch-in for Lilligant and Vivillon.
Use Sliggoo's slew of useful resistances to pivot into the likes of Magmortar, Lilligant, and Samurott. Just be sure to scout for Samurott's set first because Sliggoo is overwhelmed by Swords Dance variants. Sap Sipper gives Sliggoo additional opportunities to enter the battle by letting it freely switch into Sleep Powder users if necessary and net a free Attack boost, making its Outrage pack more of a punch. Should Sliggoo get at half of its HP or lower, use Rest to bring it back to full health so it can stay healthy to check the Pokemon it needs to. Sleep Talk should always be used during the turns Sliggoo is asleep to ensure it doesn't stay completely passive. However, in some cases when Sliggoo needs to PP stall a Pokemon such as Quagsire, it's best to not click Sleep Talk to preserve PP. When awake, try to avoid being locked into Outrage, as this can put Sliggoo into unfavorable situations. Curse should generally be saved for when Sliggoo's checks, especially Fairy-types, are eliminated, as it cannot sweep otherwise. Usually, the best course of action when against Fairy-types is to double switch out to a teammate that can threaten them. If Sliggoo has set up some Curses prior, it can also beat Steelix one-on-one and eventually start wearing it down with boosted Outrages.
Steelix is a fantastic teammate, as it switches in on Mega Audino, Clefairy, and Klinklang with little issue, all of which otherwise wall and set up on Sliggoo. In return, Sliggoo takes on most special attackers that threaten Steelix, such as Pyroar, Magmortar, and Samurott. Ferroseed functions in a similar fashion, but it provides more utility in the form of Spikes, Knock Off, and Leech Seed, chipping away at foes, while Sliggoo can easily switch into and defeat Fire-types as well as non-Calm Mind variants of Xatu. Quagsire is able to switch in on physical sweepers such as Klinklang, Barbaracle, and Malamar, all of which can significantly damage Sliggoo due to its lacking Defense before it sets up Curse. In return, Sliggoo is a superb switch-in to Grass-types, which heavily threaten Quagsire. Just note that these two are pressured by the likes of Choice Band Primeape and Shiftry, the former of which can 2HKO Quagsire with Close Combat and the latter can Knock Off Sliggoo's Eviolite while threatening to OHKO Quagsire with a Grass-type move, so pairing these up with a sturdy Fighting-resistant Pokemon such as Weezing, Mesprit, or Xatu works best. While Mesprit and Xatu cannot directly switch into Shiftry safely, they often run Colbur Berry and can act as a one time check to Shiftry.
Weezing is a good partner due to its ability to switch into and shut down defensive variants of Mega Audino with Taunt while also serving as a solid response to Fighting-types, a good majority of which can heavily damage Sliggoo with their powerful STAB moves or Knock Off its Eviolite, hindering its ability to tank attacks. Mega Audino serves as a Knock Off absorber and, depending on its EV spread, can switch into several Pokemon that can threaten Sliggoo such as Aurorus, Jynx, Gurdurr, and Hariyama. On more balanced teams, Magmortar works well with Sliggoo, as it switches into most Ice-types that threaten to break past it such as Jynx, Aurorus, and Vanilluxe, while in return, Sliggoo handles specially based Water-types that can revenge kill Magmortar.
Draco Meteor is Sliggoo's strongest STAB move and does good damage versus most neutral targets, but it has the downside of cuttings its Special Attack in half. Sludge Bomb ensures Sliggoo is not a free opportunity for Fairy-types to switch in and deals reliable damage against the likes of Lilligant and Ludicolo. Muddy Water primarily targets Steelix, which otherwise switches comfortably into all of Sliggoo's attacks, and has the added bonus of nailing Rhydon, Charizard, Magmortar, and Pyroar. Thunderbolt hits bulky Water-types, most notably Mantine and Pelipper as well as Prinplup, Samurott, and Poliwrath. Dragon Pulse can be used as a more reliable, albeit weaker, STAB attack that doesn't come with the downside of dropping Sliggoo's Special Attack. Rest can be used to bring Sliggoo back to full HP, which is especially helpful if it still needs to be healthy to pivot into Grass-types and other special attackers. Just note that during the two turns Sliggoo is asleep, it will remain completely passive.
The given Speed EVs let Sliggoo outspeed Jolly Rhydon and below, while maximum Special Attack EVs plus a Modest nature let it hit as hard as possible. The remaining EVs go into HP to provide complementary bulk. Eviolite is used to give Sliggoo a significant increase to both of its defensive stats, letting it switch into Pokemon such as Magmortar and Lilligant much more comfortably. Sap Sipper gives Sliggoo an immunity to Grass-type attacks, notably making it immune to Sleep Powder.
Use Sliggoo's set of resistances and ability to pivot into special attackers such as Lilligant, Magmortar, and Rotom. Don't bring Sliggoo in haphazardly, however, as it has no reliable means of restoring damage taken. Thanks to Sap Sipper, Sliggoo also acts a great sleep absorber, and alongside its high special bulk with Eviolite, it switches into the likes of Vivillon and Lilligant with ease. Once brought in, it's generally best to use Draco Meteor if the opponent has no Dragon-resistant Pokemon on their team. Be careful when using the move, however, as the Special Attack drop can leave Sliggoo setup bait for Pokemon such as Klinklang. Respond to Dragon-resistant Pokemon such as Steelix or Klinklang by hitting them with Muddy Water, which 2HKOes the former and keeps the latter from freely setting up Substitute. Stay away from powerful physical attackers, especially those with Knock Off, as most of them are able to heavily damage Sliggoo to the point where it can no longer reliably switch in on the Pokemon it's supposed to check.
This set is more suited for balanced and bulky offensive teams because it's played more aggressively and does not forfeit offensive momentum. Magmortar works well with Sliggoo, as it's able to switch into Ice-types that threaten to heavily damage Sliggoo, such as Aurorus and Jynx, while Sliggoo pivots into the likes of Life Orb Samurott, Ludicolo, and Floatzel. Steelix switches in on Mega Audino and Musharna, both of which can use Sliggoo to freely set up Calm Mind, while Sliggoo is able to switch on Fire- and Water-type attacks aimed at Steelix. Klinklang functions in a similar manner, though it loses to Barrier variants of Musharna and finds itself struggling to set up Shift Gear against Audino carrying Fire Blast. Weezing and defensive Mesprit both are capable of switching in on Fighting-types that threaten Sliggoo, with the former also being able to switch in on and shut down the likes of Mega Audino and Clefairy, while the latter is capable of bringing Sliggoo back to full health with Healing Wish. Kabutops and Samurott both appreciate Sliggoo's ability to pivot into and weaken faster Grass-types that can otherwise stop their sweep such as Lilligant. Rhydon appreciates Sliggoo's ability to switch into Grass- and Water-type attacks, while in return, Rhydon can use Musharna and non-Surf variants of Audino to set up either Rock Polish or Swords Dance. Mega Audino pairs well with Sliggoo, as it absorbs Knock Off and can restore Sliggoo's HP by passing a Wish to it, fixing the set's issue with being worn down.
Rock Slide can be used to deal a great amount of damage to Charizard, which can prove very helpful for taking on bulkier variants that are able to take Muddy Water. RestTalk with two attacks is also an option that lets Sliggoo immediately threaten a Pokemon such as Charizard with Rock Slide, but doing so foregoes Curse. Toxic can be used to cripple Musharna and non-Heal Bell Mega Audino, but it serves little use outside of that. Hidden Power Fire can be used on offensive sets to target Ferroseed in particular. Protect can used on the offensive set to scout the next move of a Choice item user such as Scyther or Rotom.
Fairy-types: Mega Audino and Clefairy both wall Sliggoo's Curse set by virtue of their typing making them immune to Outrage and take a pittance from Sludge Bomb from offensive variants thanks to their massive special bulk. Both can use Sliggoo to freely set up Calm Mind or support their own team by using Heal Bell and spreading status.
Ice-types: Ice-types such as Aurorus, Abomasnow, and Jynx can easily pierce through Sliggoo's high Special Defense thanks to their respective STAB attacks, though all of them do not appreciate switching into Draco Meteor or a boosted Outrage.
Eviolite Removal: Knock Off users such as Scyther, Hariyama, and Gurdurr are all able to remove Sliggoo's Eviolite, making it much more vulnerable to attacks that it'd normally have little issue taking such as Ice Beam from Life Orb Samurott. Trick works even better in this regard because Sliggoo loathes being locked into a move, neutralizing its Curse set in particular.
Taunt Users: Taunt from the likes of Mismagius, Skuntank, and Haunter stops Curse Sliggoo cold, as it cannot restore lost HP with Rest or set up with Curse and can only lock itself into Outrage, which is easily taken advantage of.

name: Goodra
smogon_description:
Goodra's ability and typing, which give it a Grass-type immunity and Electric, Fire, and Water resistances, combined with great bulk let Goodra act as a fantastic sponge that can check offensive threats such as Roserade, Raikou, Ninetales, and Salazzle and switch into bulky Water-type Pokemon such as Milotic. On top of this, Goodra's respectable Speed gives it the ability to run Choice Scarf, outpacing Choice Scarf Tyrantrum and Aerodactyl. Goodra's solid Special Attack and amazing coverage make Choice Specs also great, as it renders Goodra hugely threatening to bulky offense and balance teams by hitting a wide range of Pokemon. However, Choice Scarf Goodra is pressured by popular Fairy- and Steel-type Pokemon such as Florges and Registeel, which are easily able to switch into most of its attacks and can use Goodra as setup fodder if it isn't careful about what it locks itself into. Furthermore, Goodra has no reliable recovery and is easily chipped away by status, entry hazards, and Pokemon that it can check.
Draco Meteor is Goodra's most powerful STAB move and dishes out high damage on targets hit neutrally by it. Thunderbolt is used to hit Water-type Pokemon such as Mega Blastoise and Araquanid. Fire Blast is used for coverage on Steel-type Pokemon such as Metagross and Registeel. Earthquake allows Goodra to deal with Calm Mind Raikou and more reliably revenge kill Pokemon like Salazzle, as its accuracy is superior to that of Draco Meteor. Ice Beam can be used over Draco Meteor to hit Pokemon like Zygarde-10%, Noivern, Flygon, and other Dragon-type Pokemon for super effective damage without losing stats or having a chance to miss. However, Ice Beam is a lot weaker and leaves no real option to heavily damage foes neutral to Dragon.
Maximum Speed investment, a Timid nature, and Choice Scarf allow Goodra to Speed tie with other Choice Scarf users like Passimian and Gardevoir as well as outpace the entire unboosted metagame bar Mega Sceptile. Sap Sipper gives Goodra an immunity to Grass-type moves, allowing it to switch into Grass-types like Shaymin more easily. A Hasty nature alternatively allows Goodra to keep maximum Speed and some Attack in order to make use of Earthquake better.
Goodra should primarily be used as a revenge killer, having the Speed and moveset to take on Pokemon such as Tyrantrum, Noivern, Salazzle, and Zygarde-10%. Make sure to use Fire Blast when predicting Steel-type Pokemon that wish to take advantage of Draco Meteor. If the opponent has a Florges or Registeel, try to predict what moves to use or what switches to make in order to not waste turns dealing little damage. Even though Goodra is offensive, it can still soft check Pokemon such as Roserade and Salazzle. Try to make use of Goodra's bulk and typing to check Pokemon as well as revenge killing. Be aware of status and entry hazards when using Goodra, as it has no reliable recovery. Too much damage over time leaves Goodra open to priority users such as Golisopod, Zygarde-10%, and Honchkrow. Watch out for locking into the wrong move, like Thunderbolt against a team with Dragon Dance Zygarde-10%.
Goodra has the ability to revenge kill and force switches, so entry hazards are good because they cause chip damage to the opponent's checks. Registeel, Metagross, Roserade, and Nidoqueen work especially well, as they also cover Goodra's Fairy-type weakness. Water-types are very good alongside Goodra thanks to its Electric resistance and ability to check Grass-type Pokemon with Sap Sipper. Mega Blastoise and Golisopod work very well with Goodra offensively, whereas Milotic and Slowbro work well defensively and also cover Goodra's weakness to physical attackers. Steel-type Pokemon such as Registeel, Metagross, Bronzong, and Escavalier can switch into Gardevoir and Florges, which check Goodra. Poison-type Pokemon like Nidoqueen, Roserade, and Salazzle are also very good checks to Florges. Fairy-type Pokemon such as Florges and Gardevoir help to remove threats to Goodra like Noivern, Flygon, and Zygarde-10%. Florges and Gardevoir also have the ability to keep Goodra healthy with Wish, Heal Bell, and Healing Wish. Physical walls such as Tangela and Slowbro can work alongside Goodra well defensively, as they are able to make up for Goodra's lacking physical bulk.
Choice Specs-boosted Draco Meteor can put a huge dent into anything that doesn't resist it, being able to 2HKO specially defensive Pokemon such as Araquanid without needing to use Thunderbolt. Fire Blast nukes Steel-type Pokemon, sending Metagross packing as well as 2HKOing Bronzong. Thunderbolt deals with Araquanid more consistently and 2HKOes Milotic after Stealth Rock damage. Sludge Wave prevents Fairy-type Pokemon from switching into Goodra, as it 2HKOes Florges and OHKOes Gardevoir after Stealth Rock. Thunder allows Goodra to hit Water-types harder than Thunderbolt does. It has a chance to OHKO Mandibuzz and Mega Blastoise as well as being able to potentially paralyze faster Pokemon. Ice Beam is an option over Sludge Wave if you have teammates to exploit Florges.
Maximum Speed investment with a Timid nature allows Goodra to outspeed Pokemon such as Mega Blastoise, Tyrantrum, and Necrozma. Sap Sipper makes sure that Goodra can still check some Grass-type Pokemon such as Roserade and Shaymin.
Choice Specs Goodra is a powerful wallbreaker, hitting bulky Pokemon such as Milotic, Metagross, and Florges heavily with coverage moves as well as being able to OHKO Pokemon such as Mega Blastoise with Draco Meteor. If you wish for Goodra to break through a team easier, you will need to correctly predict in order to get rid of its checks. Sludge Wave on a predicted Florges or Fire Blast on a predicted Registeel will go a long way towards Goodra winning. Goodra still has a good Special Defense stat, so despite being offensive, it can still check a lot of special attackers like Ninetales and Roserade. Sap Sipper should be used to check Grass-types that rely on Grass-type attacks to deal heavy damage such as Shaymin and Roserade.
Choice Specs Goodra is a wallbreaker and forces a lot of switches, so entry hazard setters are very important. Registeel, Metagross, Roserade, and Nidoqueen work especially well, as they also cover Goodra's Fairy-type weakness. Goodra can remove a lot of bulkier Pokemon, leaving the door wide open for a sweeper. Choice Scarf users such as Gardevoir, Noivern, Flygon, and Shaymin can all take advantage of Goodra's ability to remove walls from the match. Both Shaymin and Gardevoir also help support Goodra with Healing Wish. Goodra still needs support to avoid being revenge killed by heavy-hitting physical attackers. Pokemon like Slowbro and Tangela can help to pivot in on these Pokemon. Fairy- and Steel-type Pokemon work well with Goodra, as they can come in on Dragon- and Fairy-type attacks that threaten out Goodra. Florges and Registeel work well defensively, whereas Gardevoir and Metagross can work more offensively. Goodra's Sap Sipper, as well as its useful Electric resistance, can help Water-type teammates like Golisopod, Milotic, and Slowbro.
Assault Vest Goodra with Dragon Tail in order to phaze checks can be used to more reliably check special attackers. However, this set is worse than both Choice Specs and Choice Scarf because it is checked easier by bulky Pokemon and its only value over other Assault Vest users in the tier is its Grass immunity. Choice Band Goodra can also be used in favor of Choice Specs to wallbreak. However, Outrage is an unreliable move that makes it easy for revenge killers to KO Goodra.
Fairy-types: Goodra, especially the Choice Scarf set, is walled heavily by Florges and forced out. The Choice Specs set is pressured and is forced into making a prediction if a Fairy-type such as Gardevoir or Florges is on the opposing team. Goodra is reluctant to spam Draco Meteor and has to get a Sludge Wave off on Florges to do anything.
Steel-types: Registeel and Bronzong are very bulky and can take multiple Fire Blasts from Choice Scarf Goodra. Goodra is forced to predict when Steel-types are going to be switched in and is pressured by this. Unfortunately, Goodra still needs to hit multiple Fire Blasts even if getting the prediction right.
Dragon-types: Goodra is very easily revenge killed by faster Dragon-type Pokemon such as Zygarde-10% and Flygon.
Physical Attackers: Due to Goodra's poor Defense, physically strong Pokemon that outspeed Goodra such as Virizion, Zygarde-10%, Flygon, and Lycanroc-D will almost always force it out.
Special Walls: Pokemon such as Assault Vest Slowking are easy switch-ins to Goodra, especially when the Choice Scarf set is used. Other Pokemon like Mantine, Florges, and specially defensive Mandibuzz can only be hit hard if hit with the correct move or if Goodra is running Choice Specs.

name: Klefki
smogon_description:
Klefki's massive utility movepool alongside its Prankster ability makes it a premier support Pokemon in the UU metagame and the best user of Spikes by far. Its amazing defensive typing alongside access to moves like Thunder Wave and Magnet Rise allows it to very adequately check top-tier threats, such as Mega Aerodactyl, Latias, Mega Beedrill, and Hydreigon. Klefki also possesses a lot of flexibility in terms of which moves it can opt to run, which, alongside its ability to set up Spikes, allows it to fit very comfortably on offensive and balanced teams alike. Unfortunately, Klefki lacks recovery, which in tandem with its subpar bulk leaves it prone to being worn down, thus preventing it from reliably checking foes it aims to check from time to time. Klefki also lacks an offensive presence, which leaves it reliant on hitting foes super effectively to avoid being too passive.
Spikes gives Klefki a way of supporting its teammates with entry hazards, punishing grounded foes that switch in and out of play. Thunder Wave cripples fast offensive threats like Mega Aerodactyl, Mega Pidgeot, and Talonflame with paralysis and gives Klefki a way of easily spreading status. Toxic cripples defensive Pokemon that may try stalling Klefki out, such as Hippowdon and Alomomola, and is also good for crippling various setup sweepers like Latias. Magnet Rise grants Klefki a temporary immunity to Ground-type moves that can allow it to ease its matchup against Ground-types like Krookodile and Gligar. Play Rough is Klefki's best source of damage against Latias, and it is also useful for pressuring Fighting- and Dark-type Pokemon like Terrakion and Hydreigon. Foul Play is also an option for punishing physically offensive Pokemon that stay in on Klefki, such as Scizor and Mega Beedrill. However, it generally isn't worth it due to leaving Klefki walled by Dark-types, and Klefki is also very reliant on Scizor setting up in order to actually pressure it with the attack. Lastly, Reflect can be used to aid Klefki's teammates in setting up or attacking against physically offensive Pokemon.
Heavy investment in HP alongside maximum investment in Special Defense with a positive nature nearly maximizes Klefki's special bulk, allowing it to check threats like Togekiss, Latias, and Hydreigon as reliably as possible. 8 EVs are invested in Speed to allow Klefki to outrun Mega Pidgeot and everything slower after paralysis. A Careful nature is used to further bolster Klefki's special bulk while preventing Play Rough's power from dropping. Leftovers gives Klefki a form of passive recovery, providing it with decent longevity. Prankster is the preferred ability, giving Klefki's status moves a +1 boost in priority and securing its niche as a reliable Spikes setter.
Klefki should look to set up Spikes early-game, as this will effectively deal good chip damage to foes throughout the course of the match. If setting up Spikes early on proves to be a monumental task, Klefki should try coming in on a foe that it can adequately tank hits from, such as Choice-locked Hydreigon or Togekiss, as this will create an opportunity to easily set at least a layer or two. Once Spikes is set, Klefki should be preserved for later on instead of being sacrificed, as it can work as an emergency check to various fast sweepers due to priority Thunder Wave and Toxic. Thunder Wave should be used against offensive threats that Klefki can tank at least one hit from, such as Mega Aerodactyl, Mega Pidgeot, Latias, and Starmie, as the paralysis will cripple them for the remainder of the match. Due to Klefki's passive nature, it should look to use Toxic to cripple various Pokemon that try setting up on it like Latias or, if it isn't using Toxic, switch out into a Pokemon capable of taking care of the sweeper it has invited in so as not to generate more free turns. Klefki should only look to attack against threats that it's capable of adequately damaging, such as Mega Sceptile, or, if it's using Foul Play, against Pokemon that try using it as setup bait, such as Scizor. If Magnet Rise is being run, Klefki should use it against Ground-types like Krookodile and Nidoqueen and Pokemon that often carry Ground-type coverage, like Mega Aerodactyl, in order to blanket check them and reliably set up Spikes.
Due to its ability to cripple fast threats with Thunder Wave while easily setting Spikes, Klefki is the main component of Spikes offense and usually fits best on offensive builds as a result. Rapid Spin support from the likes of Tentacruel and Starmie prevents Klefki from having to set Spikes more than once while also allowing it to check various threats more reliably due to refraining from taking chip damage. Cleaners like Mega Sharpedo and Zygarde-10% are fantastic Pokemon to pair with Klefki, as they can utilize its Spikes support to easily finish off weakened teams. Wallbreakers like Nidoking, Choice Band Scizor, and Terrakion appreciate the Spikes support Klefki provides them with, while setup sweepers like Infernape and Cobalion also enjoy utilizing Spikes to break past foes more easily. Water-types like Suicune, Swampert, and Mega Blastoise can switch into the Fire- and Steel-types that Klefki generally hates dealing with, while they in return appreciate its ability to switch into Grass-type attacks. Klefki appreciates Ground-type switch-ins if it isn't running Magnet Rise, which makes Flying-types like Talonflame and Moltres and Grass-types like Mega Sceptile and Celebi good options as teammates. Latias and Hydreigon have particularly good synergy with Klefki, as both resist or are immune to the types that Klefki is weak to, and they appreciate its Spikes and Thunder Wave support and ability to come in on Fairy-, Dragon-, and Bug-type attacks.
Dazzling Gleam is an option over Play Rough to more heavily damage the likes of Krookodile, Bewear, and Crawdaunt. However, it doesn't allow Klefki to damage Latias, which often uses Calm Mind, as reliably. Hidden Power Fire is another option for luring in and heavily damaging Scizor. However, it also isn't often preferred due to leaving Klefki unable to do anything to Pokemon like Hydreigon and Mega Sharpedo. A dual screens set with Light Clay is an option for giving Klefki a way of reliably supporting setup sweepers, but it is usually less consistently useful than the standard set. Defog can be run, allowing Klefki to take advantage of Prankster to remove entry hazards, but it is hard to fit on the set and removes the Spikes Klefki sets up as well as opposing hazards. Flash Cannon can be used as a Steel-type STAB attack, but it will almost never cover as many threats as either Fairy-type STAB moves or Foul Play.
Fire-types: Although they fear Thunder Wave, Fire-types like Chandelure, Moltres, and Volcanion resist Klefki's Fairy-type STAB moves and can threaten to OHKO it with their super effective STAB attacks.
Ground-types: Ground-types such as Krookodile and Mamoswine are immune to Thunder Wave and can threaten Klefki with their super effective STAB attacks. Zygarde-10% is particularly troublesome, due to its ability to ignore Magnet Rise with Thousand Arrows.
Taunt: Klefki is easily shut down by Taunt users like Hydreigon, which, upon preventing it from using Spikes or Thunder Wave, can apply heavy offensive pressure.
Defensive Pokemon: Klefki's lack of an offensive presence usually prevents it from beating most defensive Pokemon in one-on-one situations, even with Toxic. Defensive Pokemon that are immune to poison, such as Amoonguss and Mega Aggron, are particularly troublesome due to their ability to tank Klefki's hits without fear of being worn down by its status moves.
Electric-types: Electric-types like Mega Manectric and Rotom-H can freely switch into Thunder Wave and will often take minimal damage from Klefki's Fairy-type STAB attacks, which allows them to apply heavy offensive pressure to Klefki or use it as setup bait. All fear Toxic, however. Magneton is particularly annoying for Klefki to deal with, as its ability Magnet Pull allows it to trap and remove Klefki from play entirely.

smogon_description:
Trevenant is outclassed in many ways by offensive Grass-types such as Victreebel and Torterra, Ghost-types like Golurk, and Tangela in any defensive sets due to Tangela's far better defenses and reliable recovery, especially Regenerator. Trevenant's competition as an attacker all have notable qualities over it such as a better Speed tier and Swords Dance, a superior secondary typing, or Stealth Rock, respectively. Even with Trevenant's access to Natural Cure and Trick, it is not enough to warrant its usage, especially when it's pressured by Pursuit more than its competition.
Choice Band Trevenant can function as a breaker with passable coverage that can also spinblock. Natural Cure and Trick are still some features it has over its competition with status absorption and the ability to cripple a wall. However, Trevenant remains notably outdone by Victreebel and Torterra as Grass-type wallbreakers due to Trevenant's inferior typing and power, and also Golurk, which offers better utility in Stealth Rock and better coverage in Stone Edge and Ice Punch.

name: Pumpkaboo Small Size
smogon_description:
Pumpkaboo-S is one of the few Pokemon in LC with access to Z-Trick-or-Treat, the other ones being its other formes. It is the best user of the move, having the highest Speed stat. It gets many setup opportunities thanks to its great defensive typing, which allows it to check a wide variety of Pokemon. Its typing also gives it a resistance to most priority moves and an immunity to Rapid Spin. However, since Z-Moves can only be used once, it cannot use Z-Trick-or-Treat again after it switches out. Its typing also leaves it weak to Sucker Punch and Pursuit.
Z-Trick-or-Treat is a stellar setup move that boosts all of Pumpkaboo-S's stats by one stage, giving it a chance to sweep. Shadow Ball is Pumpkaboo-S's Ghost-type STAB move, hitting hard after a Z-Trick-or-Treat boost. It also lets Pumpkaboo-S get a super effective hit most of the time thanks to Trick-or-Treat's secondary effect. If need be, it can also be powered up into Never-Ending Nightmare as a last resort to nab a quick KO. Fire Blast gets rid of the Grass- and Steel-types that resist Giga Drain, OHKOing Ferroseed and 2HKOing Pawniard and Foongus, and OHKOes Pokemon such as Snover and Alolan Sandshrew. Giga Drain gets a STAB boost and hits Ground-types like Mudbray and Drilbur as well as Water-types like Chinchou and Corphish, though Choice Scarf variants of Chinchou still outspeed boosted Pumpkaboo-S and Knock Off from Corphish still does heavy damage to Pumpkaboo-S. It also provides Pumpkaboo-S with a bit of recovery.
148 Speed EVs allow Pumpkaboo-S to outspeed the entire unboosted metagame after a Z-Trick-or-Treat. 164 Special Attack EVs with a Modest nature maximize Pumpkaboo-S's damage as much as possible. The remaining EVs are used to give Pumpkaboo-S more bulk. Frisk is the preferred ability because it can be crucial in figuring out what set the opponent is running. Ghostium Z is required to use Z-Trick-or-Treat or, if the situation calls for it, Never-Ending Nightmare.
Pumpkaboo-S should generally avoid status, especially paralysis. Pumpkaboo-S should usually be saved for late-game when most of its counters are removed, such as Vullaby and Pawniard. It can also function as an early-game wallbreaker if the opponent doesn't have any of Pumpkaboo-S's counters, making it easy for it to punch holes in the enemy team for its allies to clean up. Pumpkaboo-S can reliably set up on things that it walls, such as Drilbur and Mudbray, due to its typing. Pumpkaboo-S should be careful of Sucker Punch because it deals a lot of damage, not to mention that it bypasses Pumpkaboo-S's boosted Speed. Pursuit is also dangerous, as it forces Pumpkaboo-S to take some damage regardless of whether it switches out or not. Thanks to Trick-or-Treat, Pumpkaboo-S can turn anything into a Ghost-type, making Shadow Ball super effective on almost anything. Even after it sets up, it can still use Trick-or-Treat if something new comes in.
In general, Pumpkaboo-S's teammates should be used to avoid Sucker Punch. Pokemon that can set up entry hazards, such as Dwebble and Archen, help Pumpkaboo-S get some important KOs on Pokemon such as Pawniard, which is a threat to it. Fighting-types such as Timburr and Mienfoo can take care of the Dark-types that Pumpkaboo-S fears. Water-types, such as Mareanie and Chinchou, form a good core with Pumpkaboo-S, as they can take the Fire- and Ice-type attacks Pumpkaboo-S is weak to while Pumpkaboo-S takes Grass- and Electric-type attacks in return. Chinchou in particular can also take care of Flying-types thanks to its typing. Diglett can trap and get rid of Fire-types such as Ponyta as well as Poison-types. Finally, clerics like Spritzee can heal Pumpkaboo-S from crippling status conditions as well as restore its HP.
Flamethrower can be used over Fire Blast due to its better accuracy, but its power is typically too low to justify using. Destiny Bond is an option to take an opponent down with Pumpkaboo-S as well as to play around Sucker Punch, though Pumpkaboo-S has trouble finding room for it. Shadow Sneak can be used as a priority move, but it generally isn't worth using since Pumpkaboo-S already gets a Speed boost after Z-Trick-or-Treat. Synthesis can be used for recovery, though Pumpkaboo-S has to miss out on coverage to run it.
Flying-types: Flying-types such as Vullaby and Doduo resist Pumpkaboo-S's STAB moves and set up Nasty Plot and KO with Brave Bird, respectively. However, Doduo has to be a Choice Scarf variant to avoid getting outsped after a Z-Trick-or-Treat boost and potentially KOed by Fire Blast.
Dark-types: Dark-types such as Pawniard and Houndour can switch in on most of Pumpkaboo-S's attacks and either get rid of it with Sucker Punch or trap it with Pursuit. Houndour in particular completely walls Pumpkaboo-S. Pawniard must be wary of Fire Blast on the switch in, though.
Fire-types: Fire-types such as Ponyta and Larvesta can threaten Pumpkaboo-S with their STAB moves. Ponyta has to be wary on the switch in, however, as it gets 2HKOed by Shadow Ball.
Paralysis: Paralysis hinders Pumpkaboo-S by halving its Speed, making it harder for it to sweep.

name: Pumpkaboo Super Size
smogon_description:
Pumpkaboo-XL is the slowest Pumpkaboo forme; however, it is also the bulkiest with high defensive stats, making it one of the bulkiest and best spinblockers in the LC metagame. Pumpkaboo-XL has a movepool suitable to its role as a spinblocker in conjunction with stats that make it very bulky and a decent attacker, thus making it effective at what it does. However, Pumpkaboo-XL's typing makes it vulnerable to many common types in the metagame as well as the common Knock Off, which is used by most Pokemon in the metagame.
Giga Drain is Pumpkaboo-XL's main STAB move, which lets it hit Water-, Rock-, and Ground-types such as Chinchou, Slowpoke, Tirtouga, and Mudbray super effectively, and is a semi-reliable recovery option. Pumpkaboo-XL's most reliable form of recovery is Synthesis, allowing it to maintain its longevity in battle to spinblock as long as possible. Will-O-Wisp allows Pumpkaboo-XL to spread status and cripple physical attackers, which switch into this set. Fire Blast is Pumpkaboo-XL's most powerful coverage move, hitting Steel-, Grass-, Bug-, and Ice-types such as Ferroseed, Foongus, Spinarak, and Alolan Sandshrew. Instead of Fire Blast, Shadow Ball can be run as Pumpkaboo-XL's secondary STAB move, hitting Psychic- and Ghost-types such as Abra and Gastly.
Pumpkaboo-XL's current EV spread maximizes its special bulk, since its Special Defense is lower than its physical Defense. The special bulk also allows it to deal with Staryu, a common spinner. Pumpkaboo-XL can utilize a physically defensive EV spread of 204 HP / 196 Def / 4 SpA / 76 SpD / 28 Spe to increase its already high Defense; this allows Pumpkaboo-XL to efficiently check Mudbray, as it is now more resistant to its physical attacks; however, the spread's lower Special Defense makes Pumpkaboo-XL somewhat vulnerable to special attacks. 28 Speed EVs allow Pumpkaboo-XL to outspeed base 10 Speed Pokemon such as Ferroseed. They also allow it to Speed tie with Pokemon that reach 11 Speed, such as Mudbray. Eviolite is very important for Pumpkaboo-XL, as it maximizes its defenses, which helps it maintain its longevity in battle. Frisk is the ability of choice because it can help determine the foe's set, which provides good foresight. A Calm nature is preferred for Pumpkaboo-XL, as it further increases Pumpkaboo-XL's Special Defense, making it more specially bulky.
Pumpkaboo-XL should be switched into a spinner to attempt to spinblock, allowing entry hazards to stay on the opposing side of the field. Pumpkaboo-XL can also be sent out early-game and spam Will-O-Wisp to spread burns and cripple early-game physical attackers. Pumpkaboo-XL can also switch into Pokemon that it can check, such as Mudbray and some Pokemon that have low Special Defense. It is best to keep Pumpkaboo-XL in the game until all of the opponent's spinners are defeated to ensure that the opposing side's entry hazards don't get removed. Pumpkaboo-XL should also be cautious of Life Orb Ice Beam Staryu, especially if it runs its physically defensive EV spread. Pumpkaboo-XL should generally avoid Knock Off, as it hits Pumpkaboo-XL super effectively and takes away its Eviolite, which is very important in maintaining its precious bulk.
Since Pumpkaboo-XL is a spinblocker, it would be sensible to have entry hazard setters such as Drilbur, Ferroseed, Mareanie, and Surskit as teammates. The aforementioned entry hazard setters also appreciate Pumpkaboo-XL's utility; however, Pumpkaboo-XL can also be used on teams that don't rely on stacking hazards, as it can still check some Pokemon such as Mudbray. Pumpkaboo-XL's main checks are Dark-, Fire-, and Flying-type Pokemon such as Pawniard, Ponyta, and Vullaby, which can mostly wall all of Pumpkaboo-XL's moves and defeat it easily. Great partners to check the aforementioned Pokemon are Timburr, Mienfoo, and Chinchou, as Timburr can be good on entry hazard-stacking teams and can handle Houndour and Ponyta, as it doesn't mind getting burned and can KO them; Mienfoo can handle Dark-type Pokemon such as Pawniard, but it does mind getting burned; and Chinchou can take care of Vullaby and Ponyta with its Water- and Electric-type moves as well as provide a slow Volt Switch to get Pumpkaboo-XL safely into battle if necessary. Knock Off users and Pursuit trappers can be a pain to Pumpkaboo-XL, so Pokemon such as Trubbish and Diglett can be of use; Trubbish can deal with Knock Off users easily because of its decent physical bulk and ability, Sticky Hold, whereas Diglett can trap Pursuit trappers, and most likely OHKO them, and can also deal with Fire-types and some Steel-types for Pumpkaboo-XL; Pumpkaboo-XL can deal with Water- and Grass-types for it in return. Special walls can take nearly all of Pumpkaboo-XL's moves and proceed to stall out Pumpkaboo-XL until it gets KOed (although some of them don't appreciate getting burned), so powerful physical attackers can help Pumpkaboo-XL take care of them. Pawniard also makes for a good teammate to Pumpkaboo-XL, which cannot block Defog; Pawniard can switch into an expected Defog and gain a Defiant boost in compensation for the removal of entry hazards.
Giga Drain is Pumpkaboo-XL's primary Grass-type STAB move, hitting Rock-, Water-, and Ground-type Pokemon such as Tirtouga, Chinchou, Slowpoke, and Mudbray. It also acts as a source of recovery. Bullet Seed can be used over Giga Drain because it generally hits harder, is physical instead of special, and can break Sturdy, which can be very effective against Pokemon like Onix and Tirtouga; however, Mudbray gets insane Stamina boosts from Bullet Seed and can wall Pumpkaboo-XL as its Defense rises. Synthesis is Pumpkaboo-XL's main recovery option, allowing it to spinblock consistently for its team. Will-O-Wisp allows Pumpkaboo-XL to spread burns and cripple physical attackers that may switch into it. Shadow Sneak is Pumpkaboo-XL's secondary STAB move and a priority move, which allows it to pick off weakened Pokemon and hit Ghost- and Psychic-types super effectively. Fire Blast can be used instead of Shadow Sneak to hit Steel-, Grass-, Bug-, and Ice-types such as Ferroseed, Foongus, Spinarak, and Alolan Sandshrew super effectively.
Pumpkaboo-XL's main EV spread allows it to be quite bulky, increasing its Special Defense to nearly be on par with its already high Defense, which helps it against Staryu, one of the most common spinners in the metagame. The EV spread also allows Pumpkaboo-XL to hit decently hard and outspeed base 10 Speed Pokemon and Speed tie with 11 Speed Pokemon such as Ferroseed and Mudbray, respectively; however, a Sassy nature will cut Pumpkaboo-XL's Speed to some degree. Instead of the main EV spread, Pumpkaboo-XL can run a physically defensive EV spread of 204 HP / 196 Def / 4 SpA / 76 SpD / 28 Spe, which allows it to further enhance its monstrous physical Defense to check Mudbray more effectively, but this leaves it vulnerable to powerful special attackers. Eviolite plays a large role in Pumpkaboo-XL's longevity, as it maximizes its already high bulk. Frisk can potentially determine the set of the opposing Pokemon, creating insight for Pumpkaboo-XL's teammates. A Sassy nature can be used to further enhance Pumpkaboo-XL's Special Defense giving it more bulk at the cost of its Speed, which isn't as important as its bulk. Instead of losing its Speed, Pumpkaboo-XL can utilize a Careful nature, which also increases its special bulk but lowers its Special Attack, making moves such as Giga Drain and Fire Blast less effective, so this nature is preferred if Pumpkaboo-XL chooses to use Bullet Seed and Shadow Sneak.
Like the special spinblocker variant, Pumpkaboo-XL's main purpose is to switch into spinners and prevent them from removing the entry hazards on their side of the field, which helps the sweepers on Pumpkaboo-XL's team to sweep efficiently. Pumpkaboo-XL can deal with and force out most spinners, preventing them from removing the entry hazards. Pumpkaboo-XL should be kept alive until all spinners are defeated, as if Pumpkaboo-XL faints before that, the entry hazards could be removed, decreasing Pumpkaboo-XL's team's sweeping capabilities. Pumpkaboo-XL, like the special variant, should be wary of Knock Off, as it takes away an important factor of its bulk, leaving it more vulnerable to attacks. Pumpkaboo-XL can also be used early-game to spread burns and cripple physical attackers, which renders them mostly useless.
Since this variant of Pumpkaboo-XL is also a spinblocker, Pokemon like Drilbur, Mareanie, Ferroseed, and Surskit appreciate Pumpkaboo-XL's ability to keep their entry hazards on the opposing side; however, Pumpkaboo-XL can also be used without entry hazard setters, as it can still check important Pokemon. Pawniard is a great asset to the team, as Pumpkaboo-XL cannot block Defog, so Pawniard can punish Defog users by gaining a Defiant boost as compensation for the loss of entry hazards. Knock Off users and Pursuit trappers spell trouble for Pumpkaboo-XL, so Pokemon like Trubbish and Diglett are great partners, as Trubbish can easily take a Knock Off due to its good physical bulk and Sticky Hold ability, while Diglett can trap Pursuit trappers and most likely OHKO them and can also deal with Fire-types that might pose a problem to Pumpkaboo-XL. Pokemon such as Mienfoo, Timburr, and Chinchou can deal with opposing Vullaby, Steel-, Dark-, and Fire-types for Pumpkaboo-XL; Chinchou and Pumpkaboo-XL also have good synergy, as both can deal with each others' checks, and Chinchou can provide a useful slow Volt Switch for Pumpkaboo-XL to safely enter battle.
A Trick Room set with Trick Room, either Giga Drain or Bullet Seed, Will-O-Wisp, and either Destiny Bond or Explosion with a Quiet or Brave nature and an EV spread of 44 HP / 44 Atk / 196 Def / 156 SpD / 68 SpA can be used for Pumpkaboo-XL and other slow Pokemon to sweep the opposing team, but with the loss of one of the best Trick Room sweepers, Porygon, this set is underwhelming. Rock Slide can be very effective on the aforementioned Trick Room set, as it hits Fire-, Flying-, and Ice-type Pokemon such as Ponyta, Vullaby, and Slush Rush users super effectively while outspeeding them, but Fire Blast hits Ice-types a lot harder than Rock Slide. Another form of recovery that Pumpkaboo-XL can utilize is Leech Seed + Protect, as it can drain the opposing Pokemon's health and use Protect to heal itself up safely; however, this combination is underwhelming, as it takes up significant space in Pumpkaboo-XL's moveset and is too passive in comparison to the more reliable Synthesis. Instead of Will-O-Wisp, Toxic can be used to cripple setup sweepers and can be spread early-game, crippling opposing Pokemon and some of Pumpkaboo-XL's checks. Pumpkaboo-XL can also utilize Ghostium Z + Trick-or-Treat to gain a boost to all of its stats, but Pumpkaboo-XL's bulk is much more important than stat boosts; Z-Trick-or-Treat is much more fitting for Pumpkaboo-S because of its superior offensive capabilities.
Fire-types Fire-types, especially Houndour, which has a super effective typing against Pumpkaboo-XL's, can resist nearly all of Pumpkaboo-XL's moves and likely OHKO or 2HKO it with super effective special moves without much difficulty; some Fire-types can also gain a Flash Fire boost if they switch into Will-O-Wisp, causing trouble for Pumpkaboo-XL and its teammates.
Guts Users Guts users such as Timburr and Taillow can easily switch into Will-O-Wisp because of the negligible damage a burn deals per turn and defeat Pumpkaboo-XL easily with Guts-boosted Knock Off and Brave Bird, respectively.
Dark- and Flying-types Dark- and Flying-types, especially special Vullaby, can easily deal with Pumpkaboo-XL with their super effective STAB moves, either OHKOing or 2HKOing it, and can take all of Pumpkaboo-XL's moves, although most don't appreciate being burned by Will-O-Wisp.

name: Gourgeist Average Size
smogon_description:
Gourgeist, while overshadowed by Tangela as a defensive pivot, is able to carve out a niche as Z-Move user thanks to its good Speed tier that allows it to outspeed the unboosted metagame after a Z-Trick-or-Treat, bar Ninjask and Electrode. Z-Trick-or-Treat also gives it a considerable amount of bulk and increased Attack, though it's still quite lackluster compared to that of other setup sweepers. Even though Gourgeist struggles as a defensive pivot, it's still able to wall foes like Primeape due to its Ghost / Grass typing. While Gourgeist has quite a shallow physical movepool, with its lack of a strong Ghost-type STAB move other than Phantom Force meaning it has to put up with the charge turn, it just about gets by with attacks like Return, Seed Bomb, Shadow Sneak, and Rock Slide.
Z-Trick-or-Treat boosts all of Gourgeist's stats apart from HP while also adding Ghost typing to the foe. Phantom Force is the preferred Ghost-type STAB move, but the fact that it takes a turn to charge means that it is easily exploited by foes, especially Normal-types. Shadow Sneak is an alternative, albeit weaker STAB move that doesn't require a turn to charge and gives Gourgeist priority against fast Choice Scarf users like Jynx. Alternatively, Return allows Gourgeist to hit Pokemon like Skuntank harder and gives it almost perfect neutral coverage. Rock Slide is an option to hit Fire-types, like Turtonator and Simisear.
Ghostium Z is 100% required for this set to function, as without it Gourgeist isn't able to use Z-Trick-or-Treat. Running 160 Speed EVs ensures it outspeeds all of the unboosted tier apart from Electrode and Ninjask, both of which can do little to Gourgeist. Frisk is not a very useful ability when used on this Gourgeist set, as it will not be pivoting in to try and wall something, but it's the best ability Gourgeist has access to due to it already being immune to most sleep-inducing moves. Frisk still has some utility in being able to scout the foe's item.
Gourgeist should only really be used late-game, when your opponent's team is weakened and ready to be swept, as using it early-game would generally put you at a significant disadvantage versus anything that's not offense. It should attempt to set up on something that's ineffective against it, like Primeape, and shouldn't try to boost against special attackers. Gourgeist appreciates being pivoted in by slow U-turn or Volt Switch users so that it doesn't receive any damage before being able to boost. Even though at +1 Gourgeist outspeeds almost all of the metagame, it is still slower than almost every Choice Scarf user, so it should only use its Z-Move once these faster threats like Choice Scarf Dodrio are dealt with. The same goes for physically bulky Pokemon like Gurdurr and Tangela, which should be either KOed or sufficiently weakened.
Gourgeist, even at +1 Attack, is often still very weak, so it appreciates entry hazard support from the likes of Regirock and Qwilfish to help deal chip damage on the opponent's Pokemon. Slow Volt Switch and U-turn from teammates like Lanturn and Type: Null helps Gourgeist get in for free. Lanturn additionally has great defensive synergy with Gourgeist, as it resists both Fire and Flying and offers Heal Bell support. Toxic Spikes absorbers like Skuntank greatly help during the match, as Toxic Spikes cripple Gourgeist and limit its sweeping potential. Skuntank can also trap foes with Pursuit and remove all hazards with Defog. Powerful wallbreakers like Aurorus and Zangoose are able to weaken the opponent's team enough for Gourgeist to potentially sweep later on.
Gourgeist can run Jolly over Adamant, allowing it to outspeed threats such as Choice Scarf Alolan Sandslash and Choice Scarf Kabutops; however, it really needs all the extra Attack it can get from an Adamant nature. Fire Blast with a Naughty Nature is a niche option, able to hit Pokemon like Shiftry and Alolan Sandslash, but it doesn't offer much besides that. Explosion is a potential move in the last slot, allowing for a powerful nuke. A defensive set is possible but is noticeably worse in comparison to Tangelap due to its lesser bulk and lack of Regenerator, meaning things like Hitmonchan, which Tangela counters, can 2HKO it after Stealth Rock chip damage.
Bulky Walls: Gourgeist, even at +1, struggles to break bulky walls like Tangela and Audino, both of which have ways of crippling it with Audino is also being able to recover versus it.
Grass-Resistant Pokemon: Pokemon such as Drampa and Oricorio-E are all able to reliably check Gourgeist, even when it is boosted. Drampa is the most notable, as Sap Sipper makes it immune to Gourgeist's STAB moves.
Revenge Killers: Choice Scarf Pokemon such as Rotom-F and Jynx are able to revenge kill Gourgeist, though Jynx needs prior chip damage and must be wary of Shadow Sneak variants.
Dark-types: Shiftry, Skuntank, and Absol are all able to easily check Gourgeist with their STAB Dark-type moves, with Skuntank being able to wall most variants as well. They struggle versus Gourgeist if it's boosted, however, and have to rely on Sucker Punch to take it out.
Status: Poison from Toxic Spikes, paralysis, and burn greatly limit Gourgeist's ability to sweep and put it on a timer due to it not having any reliable recovery on this set or any way to remove status.

smogon_description:
Thanks to a good defensive typing and solid stats, Gourgeist-XL is one of the premier defensive Pokemon in the metagame, capable of answering a wide variety of threats, such as Komala, Golem, physical Floatzel, non-Flamethrower Electivire, and Silvally-Fighting. Gourgeist-XL's movepool gives it access to several utility options, such as Synthesis, Foul Play, Will-O-Wisp, and Leech Seed. Notably, its access to both reliable recovery and passive recovery means it can afford to run a Colbur Berry, allowing it to easily take moves like Komala's Knock Off. Frisk is a very useful ability given that many of the Pokemon Gourgeist-XL tends to switch into, like Komala and Golem, run a variety of sets that are revealed upon uncovering their item. Thanks to Gourgeist-XL's Ghost typing, it can function as a spinblocker; it does so exceptionally well due to its ability to completely wall non-Toxic Komala, which is the best Rapid Spin user in the metagame. As opposed to other Ghost-types, Gourgeist-XL does not get Pursuit trapped very easily due to Will-O-Wisp, great bulk, and a tendency to run Colbur Berry, which Eviolite users like Misdreavus and Dusclops can't do. However, Gourgeist-XL has a lackluster Special Defense stat, and its typing leaves it weak to common special coverage moves such as Ice Beam, Flamethrower, and Shadow Ball, meaning it is easily broken with such attacks. Its weakness to special attackers is exacerbated by its reliance on Foul Play and Will-O-Wisp, leaving it struggling to hurt them significantly. Gourgeist-XL is also very vulnerable to Toxic, which is commonly seen on attackers that aim to get around it, like Golem and Silvally-Fighting. Gourgeist-XL tends to lose momentum, as it lets in special breakers like Beheeyem and Swanna largely for free, forcing its team to play reactionary.
Foul Play is Gourgeist-XL's best offensive move, allowing to avoid relying on its own uninvested offensive stats and instead use those of its target, allowing it to 2HKO Komala and Electivire. Will-O-Wisp cripples the physical attackers Gourgeist-XL generally deals with while also whittling any target down. The combination of Will-O-Wisp and Foul Play also heavily discourages physical setup sweepers like Swords Dance Bouffalant and Silvally formes from switching in or setting up. Leech Seed provides Gourgeist-XL with passive recovery and slowly wears down foes. It also makes switching out to a teammate slightly easier, as they will get some health back after doing so. Seed Bomb is an alternative in the last slot to provide Gourgeist-XL with a STAB move, notably allowing it to OHKO Floatzel after Stealth Rock.
Colbur Berry allows Gourgeist-XL to consistently switch into Pokemon like Komala, as even Knock Off won't do much damage. Leftovers is an option over Colbur Berry to increase its longevity and allow it to not use Synthesis and Leech Seed as much, though it then takes a lot from Knock Off and thus becomes easier to take down. A Bold nature is usually preferred in order to lower the damage from opposing Foul Plays Play, although Impish should be used on Seed Bomb sets in order to avoid lowering the move's damage.
Gourgeist-XL should be switched into physical attackers like Komala and Golem to prevent them from threatening its team, as it easily takes them on. In order to take these threats on, Gourgeist-XL needs to be healthy. Thus, especially if not running Leftovers, it is crucial to keep its health up with Synthesis and Leech Seed. If it is not needed to heal up, crippling a switch-in with Will-O-Wisp or Leech Seed is generally preferred over attacking with Foul Play, as this will make the foe easier to deal with for Gourgeist-XL's team. If a Pokemon immune to Will-O-Wisp or Leech Seed is predicted to come in, using the other one of the two or going for Foul Play is usually recommended. Note that Gourgeist-XL despises getting hit with Toxic, and since some Pokemon like Golem that it switches in on sometimes carry it, scouting their sets via use of Frisk and teammates is often recommended. Synthesis has low PP, so it is not recommended to use it as a method of PP stalling foes, and it should be used with care if the game is expected to go on for a long time, such as in a matchup between two defensive teams. While Gourgeist-XL can easily answer physical variants of Pokemon like Floatzel and Electivire, both of them can bust through it with special attacks in Ice Beam and Flamethrower, respectively. Thus, scouting their sets before blindly switching in is highly recommended.
Specially defensive Pokemon like Komala, Lickilicky, Muk, and Altaria can cover Gourgeist-XL's weaker Defense, while it covers physical attackers for them in return. Notably, Gourgeist-XL also covers Fighting-types like Silvally-Fighting for Komala and Lickilicky and Ground-types like Golem for Muk, while Altaria covers Fire-types for Gourgeist-XL. All four of these Pokemon can also absorb Toxic thanks to their typing, ability, or access to Heal Bell, which is very important for Gourgeist-XL. Since Fire-types like Rapidash and Simisear threaten Gourgeist-XL heavily, checks to them like Silvally-Water and Golem are solid teammates. In return, Gourgeist-XL switches into Grass-types like Leafeon that threaten them, while Golem also checks Flying-types. Similarly, checks to Ice-, Ghost-, and Dark-types like Rapidash, Silvally-Dark, and Silvally-Fighting are also all solid partners for Gourgeist-XL. Gourgeist-XL is one of the best spinblockers in the tier thanks to its high bulk, so Pokemon like Crustle greatly appreciate being paired with it. In return, Gourgeist-XL appreciates Crustle's Spikes to wear down opposing teams in tandem with Will-O-Wisp and Leech Seed. Bronzor is an excellent teammate, as it is a great answer to Altaria, while Gourgeist-XL can absorb Knock Off. In general, Gourgeist-XL fits well on Fire / Grass / Water cores with the likes of the aforementioned Rapidash and Silvally-Water, as they all cover each others weaknesses quite well.
Gourgeist-XL can function as a Trick Room setter for dedicated Trick Room teams, as it utilizes its excellent physical bulk to set up on a wide variety of threats before using Explosion to bring in a wallbreaker. However, Gourgeist-XL is outclassed by Dusknoir due to the latter's access to Z-Memento and the ability to break through Pawniard with Brick Break. In addition, it faces competition in this role from Carbink, which has access to Sturdy to nearly guarantee that Trick Room goes up. Gourgeist-XL can use Z-Trick-or-Treat to boost all of its stats and attempt to sweep, but due to its low Speed that leaves it unable to outspeed most Choice Scarf users even at +1 and lack of a good Ghost-type STAB move, with Phantom Force being its best option in a tier filled with Normal-types, there are Grass-types that utilize a similar strategy more effectively, such as other Gourgeist formes and Z-Celebrate Leafeon. Gourgeist-XL can utilize Toxic instead of Will-O-Wisp to wear down defensive Pokemon faster than a burn could, but the inability to severely cripple physical attackers makes this usually the inferior choice. Rocky Helmet can be used to punish U-turn users like Komala, but it leaves Gourgeist-XL weak to Knock Off and without passive recovery, making it less effective than the other item choices.
Special Attackers: Pokemon like Silvally-Dragon, Mr. Mime, Swanna, and Beheeyem can all break through Gourgeist-XL by targeting its weaker defensive stat with powerful or super effective moves.
Fire-types: Pokemon like Rapidash and Simisear are immune to Will-O-Wisp and can easily break through Gourgeist-XL with their super effective STAB moves, though they do not like being worn down by Leech Seed, Foul Play, and, in Rapidash's case, Flare Blitz recoil. Monferno and Combusken are especially notable for resisting Gourgeist-XL's only attacking move, allowing them to come in more easily.
Substitute and Taunt: Due to Gourgeist-XL's reliance on status moves, users of Substitute and Taunt like Vigoroth can easily cripple it and often set up on it.
Residual Damage: Toxic very quickly wears down Gourgeist-XL, leaving it unable to answer the Pokemon it wants to answer, like specially defensive Komala. In a similar manner, entry hazards like Stealth Rock and Toxic Spikes and pivoting moves like U-turn can whittle Gourgeist-XL down over time, allowing it to be broken eventually.
Flying-types: Pokemon like Rotom-S, Oricorio-F, and Swanna can switch into Gourgeist-XL with relative ease, especially since they are often special attackers, meaning they do not fear Will-O-Wisp or Foul Play, and threaten it with a super effective STAB move. Altaria can also beat Gourgeist-XL one-on-one with the combination of Toxic and Flamethrower.

Staryu's superior typing and special bulk, as well as its greater offensive presence, make it a far better user of a set like this.

name: Avalugg
smogon_description:
With great physical bulk, reliable recovery, and access to Rapid Spin, Avalugg can find itself a niche role on stall teams in the ZU metagame. Thanks to its sky-high Defense stat, Avalugg can stomach hits from a variety of physical attackers in the tier including Pinsir, Choice Band Komala, and Torterra. Rapid Spin allows it to remove entry hazards for the team, especially against certain Stealth Rock users such as Torterra, Sandslash, Marowak, and Gabite due to its great matchup versus them. However, since Avalugg is a grounded pure Ice-type, it is weak to entry all forms of entry hazards, especially Stealth Rock, and is unable to beat entry hazard setters such as Mawile, Bronzor, and Explosion Golem, thus not making it the best form of entry hazard removal in the tier. In addition, its extremely low Special Defense stat leaves it vulnerable to special attackers such as Combusken, Swanna, and Electivire. Avalugg faces tough competition as a form of entry hazard removal, as Sandslash and Komala provide better role compression and are not weak to Stealth Rock. Lastly, Avalugg is only truly viable on stall teams and requires a considerable amount of support from its teammates, such as a special wall like Bronzor, to take special hits for it.
Rapid Spin allows Avalugg to switch in on entry hazard setters such as Torterra, Sandslash, Marowak, Crustle, and Smeargle and remove Stealth Rock, Spikes, and Sticky Web to support the team. Avalanche gives Avalugg an Ice-type STAB move that move has great synergy with Avalugg's slow base Speed and high base Attack, dealing great damage if Avalugg is hit first on that turn. Toxic can be used to cripple switch-ins such as Gourgeist-XL, Combusken, and Simipour, which provides more utility. Roar allows Avalugg to phaze Pokemon that try to set up on it such as Silvally-Fighting, Pinsir, and Pawniard.
Maximum HP and Defense investment alongside an Impish nature allows Avalugg to become the best physical wall it can be to take on Swords Dance users such as Pinsir and Leafeon. Sturdy is Avalugg's best ability, as it  gives it the opportunity to phaze a setup sweeper or OHKO a threat with Avalanche such as Altaria or Marowak when at full HP. Leftovers gives Avalugg passive recovery, while Rocky Helmet wears down physical attackers using contact moves such as Komala.
Switch Avalugg in on physical attackers such as Pinsir, Komala, Torterra, and Marowak, as Avalugg can take their hits quite comfortably. Also, directly switch in Avalugg on a predicted Stealth Rock from setters that it can spin on and beat such as Torterra, Sandslash, Marowak, and Gabite. It is best to keep Avalugg as healthy as possible throughout the match, as it can continually check physical attackers and remove entry hazards when needed. Therefore, Avalugg will have to use Recover a considerable amount, potentially letting it be taken advantage of. Avalugg is also able to throw out a Toxic on a predicted switch-in as well as Toxic stall a majority of physical attackers. Use Roar to phaze setup sweepers such as Swords Dance Pinsir and Silvally-Fighting. It is best to avoid Toxic poison from Bronzor, as that will then put a timer on Avalugg. If this happens, it is best to switch out Avalugg for a Heal Bell user to cure Avalugg of status. Avalugg must also avoid taking special hits, as its poor special bulk will not allow it to take special attacks from Combusken, Swanna, and Simisear. Against these foes, it is best to switch out Avalugg for Pokemon better suited to handle special attacks.
Special walls such as Bronzor, Mareanie, and Lickilicky can sponge special attacks that threaten Avalugg; in return, Avalugg can take physical hits for them. Lickilicky is especially notable, as it also provides Wish support and can serve as a cleric with Heal Bell. Altaria and Beheeyem can beat Ghost-types such as Gourgeist-XL and Dusknoir that attempt to act as a spinblocker to Avalugg. Defoggers such as Silvally-Fighting and Vibrava can remove Toxic Spikes and Stealth Rock so that Avalugg does not get whittled down too far over the course of the match, and Poison-types like Mareanie and Muk can absorb Toxic Spikes. Silvally-Dragon, Gourgeist-XL, and Pyukumuku can be excellent partners for Avalugg, as they complement its weaknesses and can check Pokemon such as Combusken, Silvally-Water, Silvally-Fighting, and Floatzel.
Earthquake can be used to catch Pokemon such as Probopass, Combusken, Raichu, and Simisear as they switch in, as they all can take advantage of Avalugg. It is generally not preferred, however, as Avalugg must forego using Toxic or Roar in the last slot, and the utility those two moves provide is superior.
Specially Attacking Threats: Due to Avalugg's poor base Special Defense, a majority of special attackers threaten Avalugg. Combusken, Simisear, Beheeyem, and Floatzel are all examples of Pokemon that have the ability to OHKO Avalugg.
Super Effective Attacks: While Avalugg boasts phenomenal bulk, it has a poor defensive typing that leaves it vulnerable to Fire-, Fighting-, Steel-, and Rock-type attacks. As a result, super effective coverage from strong physical attackers like Head Smash Rampardos and Shell Smash boosted Crustle can eliminate Avalugg.
Entry Hazards: Avalugg is weak to all forms of entry hazards; Stealth Rock, Spikes, and Toxic Spikes are all detrimental to it in battle. This forces Avalugg to use Recover often in order to stay at as high HP as possible; thus, Avalugg can easily be taken advantage of by offensive threats, as they can switch in on a predicted Recover.
Status: Toxic prevents Avalugg from staying in for extended periods of time and prevents Avalugg from indefinitely spinning on Stealth Rock setters, as well as checking certain Pokemon such as Rapidash and Swords Dance Pinsir.

Other Flying-types like Vullaby, Doduo, and Rufflet outclass Noibat; because of their better stats and abilities, they are able to KO more Pokemon without needing to use a Life Orb.

name: Noivern
smogon_description:
Noivern's fantastic Speed tier, access to Taunt and Roost, and decent bulk allow it to act as an effective revenge killer and stallbreaker. Noivern's Speed in particular allows it to outpace the majority of unboosted Pokemon in RarelyUsed, including threats like Virizion and Salazzle. The defensive perks of Noivern's Dragon / Flying typing, notably resistances to Fighting-, Fire-, Bug-, and Grass-type moves, let it act as a workable switch-in to common offensive Pokemon, such as Virizion, Arcanine, Golisopod, and Roserade, and force prediction from stronger wallbreakers like Flame Orb Machamp. Noivern has a fully customizable fourth moveslot with options such as Super Fang, U-turn, Flamethrower, and Draco Meteor, which allows it to improve bad matchups. For example, if a wallbreaking teammate such as Choice Band Pangoro needs opportunities to break defensive cores, Noivern can opt for U-turn to give it free turns. Choice Scarf Noivern is one of the best revenge killers in the tier, able to handle extremely quick setup sweepers such as Shell Smash Barbaracle and Rock Polish Tyrantrum while still providing utility in U-turn and Switcheroo. However, Noivern's bulk, while great for an offensive Pokemon, only allows it to barely avoid KOs from attacks like Virizion's Stone Edge, so any residual damage from sources such as Toxic and Stealth Rock severely cuts into its ability to switch into threats.
Taunt allows Noivern to deal with defensive Pokemon like Mantine and prevent Pokemon like Shell Smash Barbaracle from setting up. Roost is important to keep Noivern healthy so it can beat defensive threats and pivot into offensive threats like Shaymin and Choice Specs Ninetales throughout the game. U-turn lets Noivern pivot out of walls that it struggles with such as Gyro Ball Bronzong and bring in a threatening wallbreaker to deal with them. Super Fang deals great initial damage to Steel-, Electric-, and Rock-type switch-ins like Metagross, Assault Vest Raikou, and Tyrantrum. Draco Meteor allows Noivern to nail offensive Flying-resistant Pokemon such as Tyrantrum and Mega Ampharos on the switch. Flamethrower allows Noivern to deal with more offensive Steel-types that would otherwise check it such as Metagross. When used with Rocky Helmet, it also lets it always beat defensive Steel-types such as Registeel.
Infiltrator gives Noivern a way to handle Pokemon like SubSeed Shaymin more easily and improve its matchup against dual screens teams. One can run a spread with heavy HP investment, but it'll severely cut into Noivern's ability to revenge kill and remove threats. For example, Noivern can't revenge kill Salazzle with Stealth Rock up or even beat Pokemon like Flame Orb Machamp and Roserade one-on-one without Special Attack investment. Rocky Helmet on Flamethrower sets improves Noivern's mediocre matchup against Steel-types like Registeel.
Don't switch directly into Toxic users like Registeel, as being inflicted with status heavily compromises Noivern's ability to stallbreak. Make use of Noivern's excellent Speed tier and plethora of resistances by revenge killing setup Pokemon like Virizion and checking Pokemon like Golisopod. Make use of U-turn to bring in wallbreakers such as Flame Orb Machamp and Taunt + Roost to stop walls such as Bronzong from making any headway.
Slow, powerful wallbreakers such as Flame Orb Machamp and Choice Band Metagross appreciate free turns given by Noivern's U-turn. Pursuit users like Drapion and Metagross can come in through U-turn and remove Noivern checks such as Bronzong. Defensive Pokemon like Registeel act as switch-ins to faster threats such as Ribombee and Choice Scarf Gardevoir for Noivern. There are also offensive teammates that turn some of Noivern's revenge killers into liabilities. For example, Barbaracle can set up on revenge killers like Choice Scarf Gardevoir and Tyrantrum and become a massive threat late-game. Entry hazard removal in the form of teammates such as Mega Blastoise and Mantine is important, as Stealth Rock wears Noivern down very quickly.
U-turn is great for generating momentum, giving strong wallbreakers like Roserade chances to safely switch in. Switcheroo allows Noivern to cripple defensive switch-ins such as Bronzong and Registeel.
Infiltrator is fantastic for dealing with setup Pokemon like Barbaracle on dual screens teams, bypassing the defensive boosts of Reflect and Light Screen.
Use Noivern as a revenge killer to boosted sweepers like Barbaracle and Dragon Dance Zygarde-10%. Use U-turn to generate momentum by pivoting out of switch-ins like Bronzong. Be cautious when using Draco Meteor; the Special Attack drop could cost you greatly, as it gives setup sweepers such as Ninetales free turns. Similarly, don't use Switcheroo unless all sweepers are removed, Noivern is faster than them without Choice Scarf, or you have other means of checking them.
Wallbreakers like Choice Specs Gardevoir and Choice Band Tyrantrum make use of the free turns Noivern's U-turn generates. Setup sweepers can make use of free turns given by Switcheroo. For example, Substitute Barbaracle can easily set up on a Choice-locked Registeel. Entry hazard removal from Pokemon like Mandibuzz and Mega Blastoise is very important so that Noivern can check setup sweepers like Dragon Dance Zygarde-10%, which can hit it with Extreme Speed.
Life Orb makes Noivern's Draco Meteor much more potent. For example, Raikou can't switch into it, and Barbaracle is KOed after slight chip damage. Flyinium Z improves Noivern's viability as a revenge killer and gives it a stronger offensive presence, notably allowing it to OHKO Salazzle and remove Mega Blastoise after two rounds of Stealth Rock damage. More offensive sets using items like Life Orb and Choice Specs can immediately pressure bulky offense teams using less sturdy Flying-resistant Pokemon like Metagross. Protect can be used to scout against Choice-locked attackers such as Choice Scarf Gardevoir. A spread of 184 HP / 116 SpD / 208 Spe can be used on Taunt + Roost Noivern to always take Hidden Power Ice from Choice Specs Ninetales and Life Orb Shaymin while still outpacing Salazzle.
Special Walls: Pokemon like Porygon2, Diancie, and Ice Beam Milotic have no issue switching into Noivern multiple times and removing it with their super effective attacks.
Residual Damage: Toxic is the most dangerous form of residual damage for Noivern, as it severely cuts into Noivern's stallbreaking potential. Stealth Rock and other status such as paralysis are very difficult to deal with as well.
Faster Offensive Threats: Pokemon like Ribombee, Choice Scarf Tyrantrum, and Choice Scarf Gardevoir outpace and OHKO Noivern.
Fairy-types: Florges and Diancie switch into Noivern pretty easily and OHKO it with STAB Moonblast.
Rock-types: Defensive Rock-types like Rhyperior and Gigalith can switch into any of Noivern's attacks and OHKO it with their super effective STAB moves or use it to set up Stealth Rock. Offensive Rock-types, notably Lycanroc-D, can use it to set up or just OHKO it with Stone Edge.

name: Xerneas
smogon_description:
Necrozma-DM: Necrozma-DM has the defensive typing, ability, bulk, and moves needed to check most Xerneas sets. At best, Geomancy Xerneas can 2HKO support Necrozma-DM and avoid the OHKO from Sunsteel Strike; however, +1 Z-Geomancy Xerneas is still 3HKOed. Choice Scarf, Choice Specs, and the defensive set cannot do much to any Necrozma-DM variant.
Primal Groudon: Primal Groudon resists Moonblast, is always EVed to check boosted Xerneas, and can phaze Xerneas with Roar, afflict it with status, or smack it with Precipice Blades.
Magearna: Magearna tanks even any boosted attack from Xerneas well, and it removes said boosts with Heart Swap.
Defensive Steel-types: Klefki, Mega Scizor, Bronzong, and Aegislash can survive boosted attacks from Xerneas. They can inflict Xerneas with status or hit it hard with STAB Steel-type moves. Celesteela is defeated by Thunder and Ferrothorn is defeated by Focus Blast, but otherwise they can do the same.
Ho-Oh: Ho-Oh tanks Moonblast rather well and can hit Xerneas with strong physical attacks, inflict it with status, or phaze it with Whirlwind. However, Ho-Oh is incredibly vulnerable to Stealth Rock and is typically OHKOed by Hidden Power Rock.
Lugia: Lugia checks Xerneas via Multiscale and Whirlwind, but it is KOed by a boosted Thunder after Stealth Rock.
Blissey and Chansey: Both Blissey and Chansey can stall out most Xerneas sets with Toxic due to their powerful special bulk, but they cannot defeat Z-Geomancy Xerneas on their own.
Priority: Priority attacks are typically employed by offense teams and used to revenge kill a boosted Xerneas. Users include Extreme Killer Arceus, Mega Lucario, Marshadow, Deoxys-A, and Rayquaza.
Mega Gengar: Although not a check to boosted Geomancy sets, Mega Gengar can trap and eliminate the defensive set or revenge kill unboosted Geomancy and Choice Specs sets.
Arceus-Poison and -Steel: These Arceus formes have a Fairy-type resistance and are bulky enough to check most boosted Xerneas sets, but Arceus-Steel is KOed by +2 Focus Blast.

While it is not known to evolve into or from any other Pokémon, Xerneas has two forms, which change depending on its status. When Xerneas is in a battle or a Pokémon Contest, it is in Active Mode and its horns are multicolor; otherwise, it is in Neutral Mode and its horns are cyan.
Along with Chespin, Fennekin, Froakie, and Yveltal, Xerneas was the first Generation VI Pokémon to be revealed to the public on January 8, 2013, as part of the Pokémon Direct broadcast.
Xerneas is the game mascot of Pokémon X, appearing on its boxart. Xerneas, Yveltal, and Zygarde are often collectively referred to as the Aura trio by fans.
